articles.title: Decoding Spikes From Multiunit Data
articles.content: Communication and control in biological systems is mediated by the timing of discharges –spikes– from excitable cells such as neurons and muscle fibers. Each spike is associated to a characteristic waveform that can be captured by sensors. The waveform's characteristics depend on the cell's biophysical properties and the recording modality. Depending on the technique, e.g., electrical recordings with electrodes, optical imaging, ultrasound, the observed signals are mixtures of waveforms emitted from active cells/sources (multiunit data/signals). Recovering the timing and identity of these sources (multiunit or spike decoding) is central to neuroscience, clinical diagnostics, and neural interfacing, yet it remains challenging due to waveform superposition, non-stationarity, limited training labels, and the computational demands of high-density recordings. This review provides a unified methodological perspective on spike decoding by formalizing the problem as a sparse source separation task under a convolutive mixing model. Rather than organizing the literature by application domain, we group and critically compare methods by their underlying principles: classical spike sorting, Bayesian and probabilistic inference, blind source separation, and data-driven approaches, including deep learning and hybrid schemes. For each class of methods, we present the core mathematical formulation and algorithmic strategies and discuss assumptions and limitations. Our synthesis highlights parallels in signal processing across physical recording modalities and clarifies when and why particular approaches succeed or fail. By bridging previously compartmentalized literature, this survey aims to accelerate crosspollination of ideas between application areas and to provide a roadmap for selecting, adapting, and advancing decoding methods across diverse multiunit recording modalities.

articles.title: NED-Net: an annotation-training loop for rodent EEG event detection
articles.content: Long-term EEG monitoring is central to rodent epilepsy research, and manual review is laborious because recordings span hundreds to tens of thousands of animal-hours. Published automated detectors perform well on their development datasets but are typically fixed models that may not adapt to another laboratory's electrodes, animals, or noise conditions. We introduce NED-Net, open-source software for training and maintaining seizure detectors. It uses reviewed candidate events as training labels, runs detection live during recording, and retrains as annotations accumulate. A detector trained on one mouse cohort (867 annotated seizures) achieved 93.6% precision in human review of 171 detections. Applied unchanged to a second cohort on the same acquisition system, its detections were mostly seizures (12 of 13 reviewed), but per-animal recall varied substantially (median 10%), with no convulsive reference seizure detected in four of 11 animals. Retraining with annotations from the second cohort raised convulsive recall from 15% to 64%, with at least one reference seizure detected in every animal. On recordings withheld from training, 75% of detections were seizures and 14 of 22 reference seizures were detected, whereas the source model and a model trained without these animals detected none. NED-Net supports evaluating and adapting detectors to local recordings.
articles.author: MIR, M. Y., Ledri, M.

articles.title: Repetitive suprathreshold paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation alters corticospinal excitability
articles.content: Background: Suprathreshold paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) at interstimulus intervals (ISIs) of 20-30 ms evokes cumulative online increases in corticospinal excitability. Whether these changes persist beyond stimulation remains unclear. This study investigated whether repetitive paired-pulse TMS targeting periods of net excitation or inhibition induces offline changes in corticospinal excitability. Methods: Nineteen healthy participants completed three sessions, separated by at least one week, involving 40 pairs of repetitive paired-pulse TMS delivered to the left primary motor cortex at an ISI of 20 ms (rPPS20) or 100 ms (rPPS100), or a single-pulse control condition (rSPS). Offline changes in corticospinal excitability were assessed using motor evoked potential (MEP) amplitudes recorded before and after stimulation. Results: During stimulation, MEP amplitudes decreased across trials in the rPPS100 condition, although online changes did not differ significantly between conditions. Following stimulation, MEP amplitudes were significantly reduced for up to 40 minutes after rPPS100 (p = 0.017) but were not changed following rPPS20 or rSPS (all p > 0.05). Conclusion: Contrary to our hypothesis, repetitive paired-pulse TMS targeting periods of net excitation did not induce offline changes in corticospinal excitability. In contrast, stimulation targeting long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) produced sustained reductions in corticospinal excitability, suggesting that repetitive LICI-inducing stimulation can induce lasting plasticity within the corticospinal system.
articles.author: Suresh, S., Liao, W.-Y., Thatcher, T., Villalta, I., Prowse, V., Holden, M. M., Biabani, M., Opie, G. M., Goldsworthy, M. R., Rogasch, N. C.

articles.title: Graph-Based Classification of Penetrating Arteries and Veins in Whole-Mouse Vasculature Datasets
articles.content: Advances in whole-brain imaging have produced large-scale vascular datasets, yet most lack artery-vein annotations. However, this is essential for quantitative analysis of whole brain vascular structure, blood flow simulation and translational cerebrovascular research. For unlabelled datasets, manual labelling is infeasible at network scale, and surface-vessel tracing is hampered by reconstruction artefacts, limiting the insights that can be gained from these datasets. Here, we focus on penetrating vessel trees, i.e. descending arteries (A) and ascending veins (V). A supervised Random Forest classifier is trained on graph-derived morphological and topological tree features, including persistent homology. Training uses datasets from two imaging modalities: Light sheet (LS) microscopy with arterial staining and two-photon (TP) micrscopy with manual labelling in smaller samples. Classification reached 96% balanced accuracy on independent TP dataset and 93% on LS datasets. Topological features alone achieved competitive accuracy without relying on diameter measurements, demonstrating cross-modality portability. Arteries exhibit larger diameters and longer inter-bifurcation segments, likely facilitating their functional task of directed blood delivery. The veins show greater branching complexity, allowing low-pressure drainage. These signatures are stable across modalities, supporting their physological relevance. The framework enables A-V label transfer to unlabelled whole-brain TP graph datasets, validated through the V:A ratio as a function of middle cerebral artery (MCA) distance. Operating on graph representations derived from any volumetric imaging modality and requiring no retraining, the approach is applicable to LS, TP, and likely other imaging platforms, providing a scalable foundation for A-V quantification, vascular topological analysis, and haemodynamic modelling.
articles.author: Farina, S., Greco, L., Barra, G., Boyer, M., Renier, N., Schmid, F.

articles.title: A brain signature of vaping cue-elicited craving
articles.content: E-cigarette use among young adults has grown rapidly, raising concerns about nicotine dependence and motivating a better understanding of the neurobiology of vaping. We used a cue-induced craving fMRI paradigm to develop and evaluate a brain signature of vaping cue-elicited craving, and to compare it with smoking- and food-craving signatures developed using the same analytic pipeline. Using LASSO-PCR with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, we identified a distributed pattern of brain activity that reliably predicted normative vaping craving from an independent sample (hereafter, normative craving). The vaping-craving signature was also substantially distinct from smoking- and food-craving signatures, both spatially and functionally, and showed specificity relative to previously established craving signatures. Moreover, greater signature expression was associated with greater e-cigarette dependence severity and showed a positive, though modest, prospective association with daily puff counts over four weeks, demonstrating the signature's behavioral and clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish a cross-validated brain signature of vaping cue-elicited craving, demonstrate its differentiation from other craving-related neural patterns, and link its expression to e-cigarette dependence and real-world use. More broadly, they support the potential of this framework for developing reproducible neural markers of craving.
articles.author: Zhao, S., Yu, H., Koban, L., Wang, Y., Peng, Q., Ye, T., Amlung, M., MacKillop, J., Sweet, L., Liu, J.

articles.title: Temporal instability weakens entorhinal grid-like coding in older adults
articles.content: Entorhinal grid cell representations are thought to support spatial navigation and episodic memory, functions that decline with age. Their putative fMRI correlate, the hexadirectional signal, varies markedly among older adults, but the source of this variability is unknown. Using virtual navigation and fMRI in 85 older adults, we tested whether signal strength was related to the stability of hexadirectional signals. Hexadirectional orientation stability, the cross-run reproducibility of direction-specific activity patterns, was associated with hexadirectional signal strength in the posterior-medial-entorhinal-cortex (pmEC). In left-pmEC, higher orientation stability also predicted better object-location memory. In contrast, age and local structural measures did not account for individual differences in either measure. Finally, retrosplenial absolute-orientation stability was associated with left-pmEC orientation stability, and a mediation analysis supported an indirect association with hexadirectional signals through pmEC orientation stability. Together, these findings suggest that weaker entorhinal hexadirectional signal in aging may reflect unstable, rather than absent, entorhinal grid-cell-like representations.
articles.author: Segen, V., Callau Navarro, G., Bahrd, P., Belge Bernard, T., Schinke, J.-I., Wolbers, T.

articles.title: LLM-assisted analytical review catches statistical errors that human researchers miss: documented evidence from two computational biology case studies
articles.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist with code generation and data analysis in computational biology, but their capacity to serve as analytical reviewers -- detecting statistical and methodological errors in completed analyses -- is less documented. We present two case studies in which LLM-assisted review identified consequential errors in computational biology analyses that the human researchers had not detected. In single-cell transcriptomics, review of a differential expression analysis of 22,048 cells from human striatum identified a sex composition confound (Chi-squared = 192.7, p = 8.1 x 10-44) that had produced spurious Y-chromosome gene hits; correction revealed KIF3A as the sole genuine finding (adjusted p = 1.37 x 10-14). In HRV-based stress classification, review identified subject leakage in a train-test split that allowed the same individuals in training and test sets; correction via leave-one-subject-out cross-validation produced a more reliable and higher AUC estimate (0.946 vs. 0.848). Both errors would have survived conventional peer review in the absence of systematic checking. Both corrected analyses have been submitted for peer review. These cases suggest that LLM-assisted analytical review -- using LLMs to interrogate completed analyses for confounds, leakage, and statistical artifacts -- is a practical quality assurance step that complements rather than replaces human scientific judgment.
articles.author: Chhaya, O., Ananth, V.

articles.title: Social brain fingerprinting: unique functional connectomes underpin interpersonal behaviours in non-autistic and autistic adults
articles.content: Human social interaction requires continuous adaptation while preserving stable individual patterns of brain organisation. This study examined whether functional connectome fingerprinting captures person-specific organisation during reciprocal interaction and whether its spatial architecture relates to social role and autistic traits. fMRI data from 70 adults forming 35 dyads were analysed during an iterated Ultimatum Game: 19 non-autistic Proposer-non-autistic Responder dyads and 16 non-autistic Proposer-autistic Responder dyads. Functional connectivity across 400 cortical parcels was used to assess whole-brain identifiability and edge-wise reliability. Connectomes remained identifiable across datasets, roles, and task conditions, with no reduction in global identifiability in mixed dyads. Edge-wise analyses revealed role-related and dataset-dependent differences across distributed large-scale networks. Role-sensitive connectivity features were associated with Autism-Spectrum Quotient scores, supported out-of-sample prediction, and topology-derived features classified AQ-threshold status above chance. Stable connectomic signatures therefore persist during reciprocal interaction while their network organisation varies with social role and autistic traits.
articles.author: Ielo, A., Czekoova, K., Basile, G. A., Cacciola, A., Brazdil, M., Shaw, D., Amico, E.

articles.title: The human hippocampus retroactively binds experiences across time
articles.content: Creating memories requires linking events across seconds and minutes, but canonical mechanisms of associative plasticity operate over much shorter timescales. This poses a fundamental problem: how can the brain bind information that arrives at different times? Computational model and animal studies implicate the hippocampus in associating events across time, but when the hippocampus becomes engaged and how it interacts with representations of preceding events are unknown. Here we show, using intracranial recordings in humans forming image-word associations across a ~2-s temporal gap, that hippocampal high-frequency activity predicts later memory when the second event arrives, but not during the initial image or intervening delay. At this moment, neurons tuned to the preceding image reinstate stimulus-specific firing despite its sensory absence. Across trials, hippocampal high-frequency activity was selectively coupled to this reinstatement during successful encoding and increased before spiking of image-tuned neurons. These findings reveal a retroactive mode of hippocampal binding, whereby representations of preceding events are recruited when new information arrives. This mechanism provides a neural solution for binding experiences across the temporal discontinuities that characterize everyday life.
articles.author: He, X., Petzka, M., Khazali, M. F., Brandt, A., Kehl, M. S., Kunz, L., Schulze-Bonhage, A., Staresina, B. P.

articles.title: The marginal brain
articles.content: Goal-directed cognition raises brain energy use only a few percent above resting use, a figure often read as evidence that cognition is metabolically cheap. Models of endogenous precision derive the precision of neural representations from a cost on encoding activity whose unit price is a free parameter. Embedding endogenous precision in a regulated, shared energy budget makes this cost the shadow price of energy at the margin of the budget. Neither the task share of the budget nor the net whole-brain increment identifies this price; when tasks face a common price ratio and coding technology is stable, imprecision changes by the exact fourth root of that ratio, so that the cost of information rescales while its shape is preserved; and the co-movement of imprecision and stimulus-linked task energy separates price changes from changes in coding technology. In 12,960 published estimation trials, response variance at matched numerosities rises with prior width in line with the ratios that the calibrated model predicts out of sample, and simulations indicate that a doubled price is detectable with existing paradigms when state-dependent lapses are modeled.
articles.author: Lokwani-Di Matteo, F., Sacco, P. L.

articles.title: Differential Survival of Retinal Ganglion Cell Types Following Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion
articles.content: Background. Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) is a common cause of retinal ischemia, rapidly inducing neuronal death and often producing irreversible vison loss. Interventions such as thrombolysis restore perfusion but cannot recover neurons already lost, and most patients retain permanent visual deficits. Identifying which neuronal populations die, and how rapidly, may therefore reveal timing windows and targets for neuroprotective treatment. Aims. To determine the timing of pathology, we evaluated vascular changes and neuronal degeneration in a photocoagulation-induced mouse model of BRVO. To determine differences in retinal ganglion cells (RGC) type susceptibility, we tracked the survival of RGC subpopulations using immunofluorescence markers. Methods. BRVO was induced by retro-orbital injection of Rose Bengal and FITC dextran followed by targeted photocoagulation of a branch vein. Obstruction was confirmed by fluorescein angiography and vascular damage was viewed by optical coherence tomography angiography. Cell survival was quantified by immunostaining at 3, 7, and 14 days using RNA Binding Protein with Multiple Splicing (RBPMS, pan RGC). RGC subtype markers for intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (TBR2),  RGCs (SPP1), ON OFF direction-selective RGCs (CART), and F RGCs (FOXP2) were used to examine differences in survival across RGC types. Results. Occlusion selectively disrupted the superficial and intermediate capillary plexus, sparing the deep plexuses. All examined neuronal populations were significantly depleted, but with markedly different magnitude and timing.  RGCs and F RGCs were the most vulnerable subtypes, both approaching complete loss by one week, whereas intrinsically photosensitive RGCs were the most resistant. Conclusion.  RGCs, typically resilient in glaucoma, trauma, and excitotoxicity, were markedly vulnerable in BRVO, indicating that RGC subtype susceptibility is insult-specific.
articles.author: Behboudi Tanourlouee, S., Ren, C., Santeford, A., McCracken, S., Zhao, M., Zhao, C., Apte, R. S., Zhou, C., Williams, P. R.

articles.author: McKeon, P.

articles.title: Encoding of Natural Variability in a Dexterous Motor Skill over Multiple Days in the Cortex of Freely Behaving Mice
articles.content: Skilled, goal-directed movements exhibit trial-to-trial variability even in experts, particularly in response to dynamic environmental conditions or when perfect repetition is not required for success. Identifying where, to what extent, and how stably this variability is encoded in the nervous system is essential for understanding how learned movements are robustly maintained over time yet flexibly executed on each trial. We record calcium fluorescence activity in forelimb motor cortex (M1), a key node in the multi-areal network responsible for movement control, in freely moving mice of both sexes performing a self-paced, precision reach-to-grasp task. High trial counts and rich single-trial variability enable rigorous statistical analysis of moment-to-moment movement encoding across matched behavioral sets over five days. Approximately 80% of recorded neurons significantly encoded paw, digit, and head movements during reaching, as quantified using linear models. Across days, encoding similarity shows a small but measurable decline that increases with the interval between recording sessions. This drift is heterogeneously distributed across the population, with many neurons retaining high encoding similarity even in sessions four days apart, as assessed using shuffle controls and in comparison to encoding for trial-averaged movements. Thus, over the timescale examined, M1 is capable of maintaining stable encoding of movement details at the level of single cells, even for complex, sensory-guided tasks like reach-to-grasp. Together, these results raise the question of whether downstream circuits support consistent behavior by preferentially relying on neurons with greater stability or instead through population-level readout that is robust to a modest level of representational change.
articles.author: de Laittre, E. A., MacLean, J. N.

articles.title: Motor Learning Driven by Sensory Prediction Errors Is Insensitive to Task Performance Feedback
articles.content: Accurate motor behavior relies on our ability to refine movements based on errors. Sensory prediction errors (SPEs), arising from discrepancies between expected and actual sensory feedback are a primary driver of motor adaptation. Task performance errors (TPEs), reflecting failures to achieve movement goals, also influence learning. However, whether and how these errors interact to shape net learning, remains controversial. This controversy stems from difficulties in experimentally decorrelating SPEs and TPEs, ambiguity related to interpretations of task instructions, and inconsistencies between theory and computational models. To resolve this, we employed variants of an "error-clamp" adaptation paradigm across arm reaching experiments in humans of either sex. Addressing the uncertainty regarding whether TPEs are ignored in standard clamp designs as assumed in theoretical but not computational models, Experiment 1 manipulated TPE magnitude by varying the endpoint feedback location while holding SPE constant. We found that learning was uninfluenced by TPE size. Experiment 2 assumed that the TPE is in fact disregarded under clamp instructions. To then study SPE–TPE interactions, we induced TPEs of varying sizes by "jumping" the target while always clamping cursor feedback toward the original target. Instructions to reach in the direction of the new target also then induced an SPE. Crucially, learning driven by this SPE was unaffected by TPE magnitude, a result validated by two additional experiments. Together, these results provide converging evidence that SPE-mediated learning remains impervious to variations in task performance feedback, and point to a distinction in learning mechanisms triggered by these two error signals.
articles.author: Panthi, G., Mutha, P. K.

articles.title: Conflict-Dependent Gain Control in Area VIP during Visual-Vestibular Self-Motion Processing
articles.content: Visual and vestibular signals are continuously integrated to estimate self-motion, yet these sensory cues are often inconsistent under natural conditions. How cortical circuits regulate multisensory interactions under cue conflict while preserving stable heading representations remains poorly understood. Here, we recorded neurons in male macaque ventral intraparietal area (VIP) during passive movement stimulation while systematically varying visual-vestibular heading offsets. VIP neurons exhibited strong conflict-sensitive gain modulation: congruent cues enhanced neuronal responses, whereas increasing cue offsets progressively suppressed response gain. This effect was observed not only in multisensory neurons but also in neurons classified as predominantly visual or vestibular, indicating widespread cross-modal interactions across the population. In contrast, preferred-heading shifts remain modest, suggesting that cue conflict primarily modulated response gain rather than altering heading tuning. Despite substantial suppression at the single-neuron level under large cue offsets, population Fisher information was largely preserved, indicating robust heading discriminability. Further analyses revealed flexible sensory weighting in VIP, with visual and vestibular contributions shifting as cue conflict increased. Finally, a feedforward-gated normalization model substantially improved the characterization of VIP responses by allowing cue conflict to dynamically regulate the effective normalization pool, thereby capturing both multisensory enhancement at small visual-vestibular heading offset and suppression under large cue conflict. Together, these findings show that VIP exhibits conflict-dependent regulation of multisensory gain, preserving robust self-motion representations under sensory conflict.
articles.author: Sun, H., Wang, R., Zeng, F., Chen, A.
